plan.title: Suggested plan
plan.note: For now it's based only on the martial art and the type of work. Coming soon: <ai>AI-personalised</ai> from your history and your load.
plan.sparring: {art} · sparring {minutes}': split it into rounds (e.g. {rounds}×3' with 1' rest), start at 60% and build up. Finish with 5' easy.
plan.drilling: {art} · drilling {minutes}': pick 1-2 {kind, select, grappling {positions or transitions} other {combinations}} and repeat them cleanly in rounds, switching with your partner.
plan.pads: {art} · pads {minutes}': rounds of pad work with called combinations; technique first, pace after.
plan.bag: {art} · bag work {minutes}': alternate technique rounds (precision) with power or pace rounds. Use the round timer in Tools.
plan.technique: {art} · technique {minutes}': shadowboxing in front of a mirror, working on your guard, footwork and 2-3 specific movements. No rush.
plan.conditioning: {art} · conditioning {minutes}': specific intervals (skipping, burpees, clinch, sprawls). Keep your form even when fatigue hits.

reminder.grappling: Keep your nails short and your gi/rash guard clean, and look after your elbows and knees.
reminder.strikingShins: Bring hand wraps, shin guards and a mouthguard; protect your wrists.
reminder.striking: Bring hand wraps and a mouthguard; protect your wrists.

reply.stretch: Finish with 5-8 min of gentle stretching (hips, hamstrings, shoulders, neck), 20-30 s each, no bouncing.
reply.warmup: Warm up for 8-10 min: mobility, skipping or an easy jog, and progressive sets of today's technique. Don't go into sparring cold.
reply.hydration: Sip water throughout the session; at high intensity add electrolytes. Arrive already hydrated.

info.state: Your readiness to train today, based on your recovery signals (resting HR and HRV) compared with your own average.
info.acwr: Acute (7-day) to chronic (up to 28 days) load ratio. Between 0.8 and 1.3 = safe zone; above that, injury risk goes up. It needs history: it's marked provisional until you reach 4 weeks.
info.load: Load per session = duration × RPE (arbitrary units, AU). Your Sports, MMA and Gym sessions logged with RPE are added up here.
info.monotony: How similar your daily loads are (mean/deviation over the last 7 days). Very high = little variation, more risk; alternate hard and easy days.
info.strain: Strain = weekly load × monotony. It measures your total accumulated stress for the week.

load.title: Training load
load.daysLeft: {days, plural, one {# more day} other {# more days}} of history before your week can be compared with your average: it takes 28 and you have {have}.
load.paused: No sessions in the last 7 days: the comparison comes back as soon as you log a workout.
load.empty: Log your workouts with RPE (Sports, MMA or Gym) and your load will show here.
load.soon: It turns on once you log sessions with RPE
load.gaps: Your history has weeks with no sessions (a layoff, an injury or a deload): this number may mislead.
load.context: This is a descriptive number: it is not a safety threshold and it does not predict injury. Read it next to how you sleep, soreness, fatigue and what your plan intended; if you jump well above your average, talk it over with your trainer or physio.
load.combatNote: The comparison comes from team-sport research and has barely been studied in combat sports.
load.loadInfo: Load of each session = minutes × RPE (CR10 scale), in arbitrary units (AU). It is perceived effort, not a physiological measurement, and it is not compared between athletes. Your Sports, MMA and Gym sessions with RPE add up here.
load.comparisonInfo: Daily average of your last 7 days against that of your last 28 (this week included). It needs a month of history: the 28 days are a FightLab convention, not an evidence-based minimum.
load.noVariation: All 7 daily loads are the same
load.monotonyInfo: How similar your daily loads are (mean divided by standard deviation over the last 7 days). It sums up the week's pattern; it is not a risk score.
load.strainInfo: Strain = weekly load × monotony: how much and how uniform the week was. It is descriptive and has no thresholds.
load.bigJump: Big jump: 30% or more above your average.

coach.briefingUp: Your week is {pct}% above your 4-week average. It is not an injury warning: check how you feel and, if it is a big jump, talk it over with your trainer.

cut.title: Making weight: information, not a protocol
cut.intro: FightLab gives no cutting or rehydration protocols. This is what the evidence says:
cut.planned: Sports-medicine consensus (ACSM, 2021) prefers gradual, planned weight management, and choosing a weight class you can reach without undue physical, nutritional or psychological stress.
cut.common: Losing a lot of weight in a few days is common in combat sports, most of all in MMA, but being common does not make it safe.
cut.noSafePct: Its effects on performance are mixed and no percentage of loss is safe.
cut.regain: Getting the weight back on the scale after the weigh-in does not prove that you are rehydrated or ready to compete.
cut.deaths: Sauna, sweat suits and training in hot rooms to force the loss are the methods linked to deaths.
cut.noWater: Water loading, diuretics, laxatives, vomiting or IV fluids are not options FightLab puts forward: diuretics and IV fluids are banned in most sports. If someone suggests them, talk to a doctor or a sports dietitian.
cut.rules: Passing the weigh-in or a hydration test does not mean you are fine. Check the rules of your event and your federation.
cut.recovery: For recovery after the weigh-in, consensus gives only general guidance, largely from other sports; any individual plan belongs with a sports dietitian.
cut.emergency: If someone collapses or is confused during a cut, it is an emergency: call emergency services. Also stop and seek medical care with chest pain or an irregular heartbeat, severe dizziness or fainting on standing, vomiting that does not stop, severe cramps, very dark or scant urine, or if you cannot keep fluids down.
cut.refer: For your plan: a sports dietitian or a sports physician.
cut.minor: Sports-medicine consensus discourages making weight in young athletes, so FightLab shows no weight-cut information to under-18s. Talk to your doctor or a sports dietitian.
cut.footer: Weigh-in: target and countdown. FightLab gives no cutting or rehydration protocols.
cut.briefing: Weigh-in in {days} days and you are {over} kg from your target. To get there, consensus prefers gradual, planned weight management: ask a sports dietitian for your plan.
cut.recTitle: {over} kg above target · weigh-in in {days} d
cut.recWhy: FightLab gives no cutting protocols. Consensus (ACSM) prefers making weight gradually and with a plan, and dehydration cuts carry health and performance costs. For a plan, a sports dietitian or your doctor.
cut.replyOver: You are {over} kg from your target with {days} days to go. I won't give you a cutting protocol: consensus prefers a gradual, planned loss, and a sports dietitian is the right person for your plan.

head.title: Blow to the head
head.intro: If you took a blow to the head (or a hard blow that jolted your head), report it here.
head.report: Report a blow to the head
head.symptomsQ: Do you have any symptom, or has someone seen signs in you?
head.symptomsHint: Headache, dizziness, nausea, blurred vision, balance problems, feeling off, confusion, memory gaps, fatigue or irritability; or lying still, being slow to get up, unsteady or dazed.
head.redFlagsHint: Neck pain, a seizure, passing out, vision problems, worsening confusion or headache, or repeated vomiting.
head.error: The report could not be saved. Please try again.
head.emergencyNow: Get emergency care now. Do not stay alone, do not drive and do not go home alone.
head.noSymptoms: Saved. Feeling fine after sparring does not rule out a head injury: if any symptom shows up in the next hours or days, stop training and report it here.
head.crt6: Full list of warning signs: Concussion Recognition Tool 6 (CRT6), official document
head.blockedBody: You reported a blow to the head with symptoms. A doctor needs to check it and decides whether it is a concussion. Until a clinician clears you: no sparring, clinch, partner drills or live grappling. Walking and everyday activity are fine if they do not clearly worsen your symptoms.
head.stepsTitle: How the return to contact works
head.stepsNote: Each step takes at least 24 hours, so a full return takes at least about a week and is usually done within a month. A clinician supervises and authorises the contact steps; FightLab computes no dates. If your symptoms are not clearly improving after 2-4 weeks, ask for a fuller evaluation.
head.stepsMap: In FightLab, solo technical work counts as step 3, cooperative drills without head contact as step 4, and sparring or live rolling as step 5.
head.clearConfirm: I confirm that a doctor or other clinician has cleared me to return to contact
head.clearNote: This is the only way to lift the block: FightLab never lifts it on a timer.
head.contactNote: Contact is blocked because of a blow to the head: you can log what you already did, but do not do this work until a clinician clears you.
head.noContactPlan: With contact blocked because of your blow to the head I won't suggest {work}. Today, if your symptoms allow it, solo and easy work; a clinician decides the return to contact.
head.headgear: Headgear mainly prevents cuts; it has not been shown to prevent concussion.

signs.title: Warning signs
signs.intro: Tick only what is happening. If you are unsure, read the description again; if it is still unclear, do not tick it and act on it as soon as it appears.
signs.cardiac: Chest, neck, jaw or arm pain or pressure, breathlessness, dizziness or fainting, or palpitations (during exercise or at rest)
signs.cardiacEmergency: It is chest pain at rest, fainting, or chest pain with breathlessness and sweating
signs.systemic_illness: Fever, aches all over, or feeling unwell below the neck
signs.head_cold: Just a head cold (runny nose or sore throat, no fever or aches)
signs.disordered_eating: Vomiting, laxatives or diet pills, exercising to make up for food, bingeing with loss of control, or a marked fear of gaining weight
signs.disorderedUrgent: Also: fainting, confusion, eating almost nothing for 2 days or more, or vomiting several times a day
signs.rhabdo: Very sore, weak or swollen muscles with dark urine after training
signs.injury: New pain or an injury in some area
signs.injurySevere: The pain is sharp or getting worse, or I have numbness or weakness

readiness.no_data: Not enough data yet to compare you with yourself. A few days of check-ins will fix that.

gymImport.title: Import workouts
gymImport.subtitle: Upload the CSV your gym app exports. The sets go into your history and count towards strength and your plan.

help.hevy: Hevy: Settings › Export Data. Kilograms or pounds both work.
help.generic: Generic CSV: columns date (YYYY-MM-DD, or YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM for two sessions on one day) and exercise. Optional: weight_kg or weight_lbs, reps, rir, rpe, set_type, distance_km, duration_s, session and notes. Use a full stop for decimals (12.5).
help.lyfta: Lyfta: there is no importer yet. To bring it in: export your Lyfta workouts as CSV, keep one row per set, rename the columns to date (YYYY-MM-DD), exercise, weight_kg and reps (the other generic CSV columns are optional), delete the rest and upload it as “Generic CSV”.
